concept.title: Optimizing Wi-Fi Performance
concept.shortdesc: Optimize the Wi-Fi network to improve wireless coverage, connection stability, and network performance for connected devices.

conbody.p: Wi-Fi performance depends on the location of the , the selected Wi-Fi band, wireless interference, the distance between devices, and the number of connected devices.
Evaluate these factors before you change the wireless configuration or add network equipment.

section.title: Factors That Affect Wi-Fi Performance
section.p: The following factors can affect wireless coverage and connection quality:

ul.li: The location and height of the
The distance between the router and client devices
Walls, floors, furniture, and other physical obstructions
Interference from appliances and nearby wireless networks
The capabilities of the router and client devices
The number of devices that use the network at the same time
The type and amount of network traffic

section.note: Start with the location of the router. A central and open location can improve Wi-Fi coverage without changes to the network settings.
Measure signal strength, channel utilization, connection stability, and throughput before and after you change the network configuration.

section.title: Router Placement
section.p: Place the near the center of the required coverage area. Use an open and elevated location.
Keep the router away from large metal objects, enclosed cabinets, heat sources, water, and devices that can cause wireless interference.

section.title: Wi-Fi Band Selection
section.p: The supports . Each band provides different coverage and performance characteristics.
The 2.4 GHz band usually provides more coverage and supports many older devices. The 5 GHz band usually provides higher data rates over a shorter distance.
section.note: Keep both supported Wi-Fi bands enabled when possible. This setting gives client devices more connection options.
Evaluate client capabilities, channel utilization, signal strength, and application requirements before you assign devices to a specific band.

section.title: Wireless Interference
section.p: Wireless interference can reduce network speed and cause unstable connections.
Potential sources of interference include nearby Wi-Fi networks, microwave ovens, cordless telephones, wireless cameras, Bluetooth devices, and some smart home devices.
Increase the distance between the and potential sources of interference. Change the wireless channel only when the current channel has persistent interference.
section.note: Review channel utilization before you select manually. Use automatic channel selection when interference conditions change frequently.

section.title: Wi-Fi Coverage Extension
section.p: A single router might not provide sufficient coverage in a large home, a multistory home, or a building with dense construction materials.
Use the when a wired Ethernet connection is available in the area that requires additional coverage. Use the when multiple wireless coverage points are required.
section.note: Put an access point or mesh node in a location that has a reliable connection to the main router. Do not put the device inside the area where the Wi-Fi signal is already unusable.
Use a wired backhaul connection when possible. A wired backhaul can provide more consistent performance than a shared wireless backhauls.

section.title: Performance Evaluation
section.p: Test the Wi-Fi connection in the locations where users frequently connect wireless devices.
Check the signal strength, connection stability, and network performance. Test more than one client device because device capabilities can affect the results.
section.note: Test the connection with a smartphone, tablet, or laptop. Confirm that the device remains connected in each required coverage area.
Record the test location, frequency band, channel, signal strength, throughput, latency, and packet loss. Use the same test conditions when you compare results.
section.p: If the connection remains slow or unstable after optimization, refer to the applicable troubleshooting topic.
